**Operations Improvement Plan: From 14-Week Quoted Lead Time to a Competitive, Quality-Protected 6–8 Week Promise** --- ### 1. Root-Cause Diagnosis: Where the 14 Weeks Are Actually Lost In industrial equipment manufacturing, actual touch-time is typically only 10–20 % of the total quoted lead time. The remainder is hidden “wait and wander” created by functional silos. Based on the symptoms (serial inspections, inter-departmental blame, and inventory buffers), the 14 weeks are consumed roughly as follows: | Phase | Typical Time Loss | Root Cause | |-------|-------------------|------------| | **Pre-production** (Weeks 0–3) | Spec re-work, BOM clarification, and raw-material procurement | Sales promises custom configurations without real-time production input; long-lead castings/forgings are not ordered until a firm PO is received. | | **Fabrication & Machining** (Weeks 3–7) | Queues between departments | Large transfer batches, functional departmental layout (job-shop syndrome), and machines scheduled for efficiency (large batches) rather than flow (small batches). | | **In-Process Quality** (Weeks 5–8) | Inspection queues | Inspectors are a shared, under-resourced pool; parts sit for days awaiting dimensional or NDT sign-off. The *dwell* time is treated as “free” until the schedule slips. | | **Warranty-Inducing Rework** (Hidden inside weeks 6–10) | Unplanned loops | Defects discovered late—after assembly or during final test—trigger teardowns. The last compression attempt likely skipped early-stage error-proofing, converting inspection time into failure spikes. | | **Final Certification & Test** (Weeks 9–12) | Serial, end-of-line gates | All certified inspections (fatigue, pressure, electrical safety, material certs) are performed sequentially after assembly, monopolizing scarce test rigs. | | **Shipping & Customer Buffer** (Weeks 12–14) | Padding | Because the system is unreliable, the quoted schedule includes a hidden 2-week safety buffer that competitors have already engineered out. | **The key insight:** You do not have a 14-week *production* problem; you have a 14-week **systemic queue and coordination** problem. The competitor’s 6 weeks is likely achieved through assemble-to-order (ATO) platforms, synchronized quality, and supplier decoupling—not by eliminating inspections. --- ### 2. The Improvement Architecture: Five Interdependent Levers #### A. Process Redesign: Create Flow, Not Batches - **Value Stream Mapping (VSM):** Map the current state for the top two product families that represent ~80 % of volume. Identify every physical inventoried queue. - **Cellular / Pulse Flow:** Group machines and assembly stages into focused product cells where feasible. Where products are too large to move quickly, create fixed “pulse lines” with defined FIFO lanes and **WIP caps**; when a lane hits its cap, the upstream process stops until the bottleneck is cleared. - **Overlap Operations:** Begin sub-assembly fabrication and long-lead purchased components *before* the final design is fully frozen for standard options (see Postponement, below). - **Setup Reduction (SMED):** Apply single-minute exchange of die discipline to machine changeovers to economically justify smaller production batches without sacrificing throughput. #### B. Inventory Strategy: Strategic Decoupling (The Postponement Model) Pure make-to-order (MTO) is incompatible with a 6-week market standard if raw materials alone take 8 weeks. Shift to a **configure-to-order (CTO)** posture: - **Platform Inventory:** Hold strategically “barely finished” subassemblies and base frames in inventory, completing only the final 15–25 % of customization after order entry. This converts 8–10 weeks of build time into 2–3 weeks of final configuration. - **Long-Lead Raw Material Buffers:** For unique castings or motors that still exceed target lead times, place semi-forecast-driven blanket orders with suppliers; pull against those blankets when a firm order arrives. The financial risk is managed by standardizing designs so the material is usable across multiple end-item configurations. - **Finished Goods for “Runners”:** For the most common variant, hold one or two units of finished goods. Sales can quote immediate delivery (0–1 week) on those SKUs, instantly stopping competitive losses on the most frequent deals. #### C. Scheduling: From Infinite MRP to Finite-Capacity, Quality-Synchronized Planning - **Capable-to-Promise (CTP):** Replace the static 14-week quote with a dynamic scheduling engine. When an order arrives, the system checks (a) availability of platform subassemblies, (b) supplier material buffers, and (c) finite capacity on the final assembly/test line. Sales quotes a date based on **actual** load, not averages. - **Quality as a Scheduled Resource:** Treat inspectors and test rigs as production resources in the ERP schedule. Book inspection slots just like machine time so that “waiting for quality” is no longer an unplanned black hole. - **Visual Pull & WIP Caps:** Use kanban or POLCA (Paired-cell Overlapping Loops of Cards with Authorization) to control release of work into the shop. The fastest way to add lead time is to release every order on the floor at once; WIP caps force throughput by finishing what was started. #### D. Supplier Re-Engineering - **Supplier Quality Certification & Ship-to-Stock:** Move incoming inspection out of your receiving bay and into your supplier’s process. Audit and certify top suppliers so material flows directly to point-of-use, cutting 3–5 days of receiving and IQC queue per shipment. - **Lead-Time Compression Contracts:** For the 10 longest-lead items, negotiate vendor-managed inventory (VMI) or consignment arrangements. Share demand forecasts and give suppliers 12-month visibility with 2-week firm-call-off windows. - **Localization / Dual Sourcing:** Where a single overseas supplier drives 8-week material starvation, qualify a regional second source even at a slight premium; the premium is paid back by higher win rates and reduced expediting. --- ### 3. Protecting Certified Quality: The “No-Compromise” Protocol The organization’s trauma from the last compression attempt means any proposal to touch quality processes will face justified skepticism. Quality is protected through **relocation and error-proofing**, not dilution. | Principle | Implementation | How It Protects Certification | |-----------|----------------|------------------------------| | **Gate Relocation, Not Removal** | Move inspections from end-of-line to **point-of-creation** (e.g., weld NDT at the weld cell, dimensional CMM at the machining center). | Certifications are still performed; they simply happen in parallel with production rather than after it. | | **Certify the Process** | Once a process demonstrates capability (Cpk ≥ 1.67 on critical characteristics), shift from 100 % inspection to **statistical process control (SPC)** with digital auto-gaging. Maintain full traceability and audit trails. | The *standard* remains certified; the method shifts from reactive inspection to preventive process control, which certifying bodies accept when documentation is rigorous. | | **Digital Quality Thread** | Replace manual C-of-C paperwork with automated data collection (CMM, torque logs, NDT images) uploaded to a job-level digital dossier. | Inspector time shifts from “writing reports” to “auditing data,” cutting queue time without cutting evidence. | | **Poka-Yoke & Self-Inspection** | Fit workstations with go/no-go gauges and vision systems. Train and certify *operators* to perform first-off and in-process checks; QA audits the operator and the data. | Quality ownership is embedded at the source. QA becomes an audit/enablement function rather than a bottleneck. | | **Sacred Final Gates** | Statutory tests (e.g., 72-hour pressure cycling, customer-witness inspections) keep their full durations. However, start subassembly endurance tests **earlier** using parallel methodology, so that only the final integration test remains on the critical path. | Test rigor is unchanged; only the *calendar position* of the test changes. | | **Hard Warranty Phase-Gate** | Pilot any lead-time change on one product family and monitor external failure rates for a minimum of 90 days post-shipment. If warranty claims rise above the current baseline, the change is halted and root-caused (8D) before scaling. | Prevents the “speed at all costs” failure mode that damaged the brand previously. | --- ### 4. Aligning Production, Quality, and Sales: Ending the Feud Functional warfare thrives when each department optimizes its own silo at the expense of the system (e.g., Production maximizes machine utilization with huge batches; Sales maximizes revenue with optimistic promises; Quality maximizes inspection thoroughness with infinite queues). Alignment requires **shared accountability for system throughput**. #### A. Governance: The Customer Fulfillment Council - **Executive Sponsor:** A COO or VP of Operations chairs a weekly **Customer Fulfillment Council** with equal-weighted authority for the heads of Production, Quality, and Sales. - **Charter:** The council owns one metric: **Perfect Order Rate** (On-time × In-full × Zero defects × Correct documentation). No single function wins unless the system wins. - **Decision Rights:** Quality retains veto power over any change that risks certification or warranty performance, but must issue a “qualified yes with conditions” within 48 hours or escalate to the COO. Production owns the scheduling cadence; Sales owns the order-intake and promise accuracy. #### B. Metrics & Incentives (Tied to Collective Bonus) | Function | Old Silo Metric | New System Metric | |----------|---------------|-------------------| | **Sales** | Revenue / bookings | *Quote Accuracy* (promise date vs. actual ship), *Win Rate on Delivery*, and *Gross Margin* (penalize custom specs that break the platform model) | | **Production** | Labor efficiency / overhead absorption | *Manufacturing Critical-Path Time (MCT)*, *Schedule Adherence*, *First-Pass Yield* (absorption accounting is revised to reward flow, not just machine hours) | | **Quality** | Inspection pass rate / internal PPM | *Cost of Quality* (prevention + appraisal + failure), *External Warranty Events*, *Inspection Cycle Time* (time from request to sign-off) | #### C. The “Promise-to-Ship” Protocol (Joint Front-End Process) Within 24 hours of order receipt: 1. **Sales** enters the configuration into the CTP engine. 2. **Production** validates platform availability and line capacity. 3. **Quality** validates the certification path (which tests are needed, which are already pre-cleared by platform build). 4. All three e-sign a **Fulfillment Commitment** delivered to the customer. No单方面 (unilateral) promise changes. #### D. Transparency: Make the Blame Impossible - Install a **digital order tracker** (Andon-style) visible to all three functions. When an order waits more than 4 hours at any station, it flags the *stage*, not the *person*. - Hold monthly “Voice of Customer” sessions where Sales presents the actual win/loss data—naming which deals were lost to the competitor’s 6-week delivery—directly to Production and Quality. Emotional and factual alignment accelerates when all three see the lost order folders. --- ### 5. Implementation Roadmap | Phase | Timeline | Objective | Key Actions | |-------|----------|-----------|-------------| | **Phase 1: Stabilize & Diagnose** | Months 1–2 | Stop the bleeding; map reality | • VSM the top 2 families
• Implement WIP caps and visual flow
• Launch Customer Fulfillment Council
• Deploy CTP logic for new quotes (do not change market-facing lead time yet) | | **Phase 2: Quality Flow & Supplier Decoupling** | Months 3–5 | Protect quality while freeing inspection time | • Relocate quality gates to point-of-creation
• Launch certified supplier program (top 10 items)
• Begin raw-material postponement buffers
• Digitize inspection records | | **Phase 3: Compress Non-Quality Time** | Months 6–9 | Reduce queues, batches, and supplier lead time | • Reduce transfer batches / implement FIFO lanes
• Synchronize QA resources in finite schedule
• Roll out platform postponement (CTO) for standard models
• Cross-train operators for self-inspection | | **Phase 4: Validate & Scale** | Months 10–12 | Prove safety, then promise speed to market | • Monitor warranty rates on pilot family; if clean, approve
• Adjust standard quoted lead time: **first to 9 weeks**, then to **7 weeks**; reserve 6 weeks for ATO/platform orders only
• Roll out to remaining product families | **Target Outcomes:** - **Month 6:** Internal MCT reduced to 9 weeks; pilot family warranty rate flat or improved. - **Month 12:** Standard quoted lead time reduced to **7 weeks**; platform orders quoted at **4–5 weeks**. - **Year 2:** Achieve **6 weeks** on ATO lines through continued supplier lead-time reduction and test-rig automation. --- ### 6. Risk Mitigation: Why This Time Is Different The previous failure likely stemmed from telling Production “ship faster,” which translated into skipping checks and hiding WIP. This plan avoids that through: - **WIP Caps:** Prevents the floor from becoming an uncontrolled expedite mess. - **Warranty Phase-Gates:** Lead time is not quoted to the market until the pilot proves itself. - **Quality as Co-Designer:** Quality engineers help redesign the flow; they do not rubber-stamp a Production plan imposed on them. - **Sales Discipline:** The CTP tool prevents Sales from writing checks the factory cannot cash, eliminating the root cause of emergency shortcuts. --- ### 7. Summary You can cut lead time from 14 weeks to **7 weeks (and selectively to 6)** without dismantling certified quality. The path is not “inspect less” but **inspect earlier, flow faster, decouple suppliers, and promise smarter**. - **Time is lost in queues** between silos, not in value-add work. - **Process** changes focus on cellular flow and small batches. - **Inventory** changes use postponement and platforms to collapse the front end. - **Scheduling** changes treat quality capacity as a finite, planned resource. - **Supplier** changes move inspection upstream and bring material lead times inside the评选 window. - **Quality** is protected by relocating gates to the source, digital traceability, and a hard warranty firewall. - **Alignment** is achieved by a shared Perfect Order metric, a CTP promise protocol, and cross-functional governance that makes system success the only scorecard. The competitor’s 6-week quote is not magic; it is the output of a system designed for flow. Rebuild the system as described, and the 14-week quote becomes a relic of the past—without repeating the warranty disasters of the past.
